documents.title: European urinalysis guidelines automated sediment analysis

chunks.content: Abbreviations AP Amorphous phosphate AUC Area under curve BAC Bacteria CaOx Calcium oxalate CI Confidence interval CLSI Clinical laboratory standards institute CV Coefficient of variation ESD Extreme studentized deviate GC Granular cast HC Hyaline cast HPF High power field LPF Low power field LC Leukocyte cluster MT Mucous thread NLR Negative likelihood ratio NPV Negative predictive value PLR Positive likelihood ratio PPV Positive predictive value RBC Red blood cell RTEC Renal tubular epithelial cell SEC Squamous epithelial cell SG Specific gravity UTI Urinary tract infection WBC White blood cell YLC Yeast like cell 1 Introduction Urinalysis is the third most ordered test group after clinical chemistry and complete blood count in clinical laboratories. It is still a valuable test especially in the screening, monitoring and follow-up of kidney, urinary tract, liver diseases to identify metabolic, cholestatic and haemolytic disorders. The diagnostic approach is based on visual inspection, chemical analysis and enumeration of urine particles via sediment examination [ ]. While chemical analysis is performed via pad-based strip technology, sediment examination is carried out by either digital image processing and particle recognition or flow cytometry methods [ ]. Many manufacturers have developed automated urine analysis platforms for use in clinical laboratories. There are basically two different detection methodologies for particle identification such as imaged-based or flow cytometry. Image-based systems classify particles according to particle size, shape and texture features. In flow cytometry technology, cells are stained with two different dyes and identified with additional properties such as electrical impedance and light scatter [ ]. The best candidate reference measurement procedure of urine sediment examination was defined as “chamber counting of uncentrifuged urine specimen via phase contrast microscopy with supravitally staining the particles” especially for renal components [ ]. Although manual microscopy is considered as gold standard method for urine sediment analysis, it is not an effective, practical and applicable technique due to the high inter- and intra-individual variability, the need for expertise and preanalytical variables in sample preparation causing cell destruction [ ]. These limitations affect the precision and accuracy of urine sediment analysis. Guidelines such as CLSI GP16-A3 [ ] and European Urinalysis Guideline [ ] have been published for urinalysis process standardization. Automated urine sediment analyzers significantly reduce turnaround times in high-volume laboratories. Automatic strip readers and particle analyzers are mechanically integrated to provide the laboratory workflow, allowing the user to identify cases that need manual review [ ]. Therefore, automated walk-away urine analyzers are emerging as an alternative tool. However, it is critical to benchmark these platforms before implementation to clinical laboratory. Our aim was to compare the results of Labsan Trion and Dirui FUS-200/H-800 devices with manual microscopy. In our best knowledge, this is the first report comparing Labsan Trion TriCell-1000 automated urinalysis system with FUS-200/H-800 device. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study population This prospective, randomized, observational, comparative study included a total of 463 freshly obtained out- and in-patient routine urine samples admitted to clinical laboratory in January 2023 at Selcuk University Faculty of Medicine, Konya, Turkey. Although a small-scale comparative study would be sufficient for many urine analyzers to demonstrate the capability of system to detect and count the particles in urine with acceptable precision and accuracy [ ], a large-scale study was designed. Randomly selected first morning, 50 mL mid-stream urine samples were collected into sterile containers and analyzed within 1 h according to Clinical Laboratory Standards Institute GP16-A3 guidelines [ ] and European Urinalysis Guidelines [ ], respectively. The study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee and performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. 2.2 Automated testing methods Chemical analysis was performed with Dirui H10-800 (Lot No: 20220112J5) and Trion URS-11L (Lot No: 202203U11) strips, respectively. Both devices perform strip analysis and specific gravity using reflectance photometry and refractometry, respectively. Analyzers based on digital image processing and particle recognition automatically display the cells in a flowing sheath fluid mixed monolayer urine sample, take the pictures of particles via digital camera, analyse these pics with a particle recognition software, transfer images of the formed elements to the screen and allow well-trained personnel to select, reclassify or remove them. Trion and Dirui systems include two combined units as TRICHEM-100 (Chemical), TRISED-100 (Sediment) and H800 (Chemical), FUS-200 (Sediment), respectively. Technical specifications of the devices were presented in . Calibration, maintenance and control procedures of all devices were completed and made ready to provide patient results before the study. 2.3 Manual microscopic examination Particle analysis via manual microscopy was performed according to CLSI GP16-A3 guidelines. Briefly, 12 mL urine sample was centrifuged at 400 g for 5 min (Sigma 3K30, Germany centrifuge). 11 mL supernatant was discarded. The remaining 1 mL of sediment was homogeneously mixed. H800 (Chemical), FUS-200 (Sediment), respectively. Technical specifications of the devices were presented in . Calibration, maintenance and control procedures of all devices were completed and made ready to provide patient results before the study. 2.3 Manual microscopic examination Particle analysis via manual microscopy was performed according to CLSI GP16-A3 guidelines. Briefly, 12 mL urine sample was centrifuged at 400 g for 5 min (Sigma 3K30, Germany centrifuge). 11 mL supernatant was discarded. The remaining 1 mL of sediment was homogeneously mixed. Final pipetting urine volume for manual microscopy was calculated as [ ]: HPF area = π*r 2 [(π = 3.14; r (diameter of one square ∼ 0.15 mm)] as HPF area = 3.14*0.15*0.15 = 0.070 mm 2 2.3.1 Total area of microscopic slide = 24 mm*32 mm = 768 mm<sup>2</sup> Number of HPF = Total area of slide/HPF area Number of HPF = 768/0.070 = 10,971. To obtain 4000 HPF/mL, the final amount of sediment for 1 mL (1000 μL) centrifuged urine sediment was calculated as 10,971/4000 = 2.74 fold. 2.3.2 25 μL of 1 mL urine sediment represents 4000 HPF/mL and 25/2.74 = 9.12 μL–9 μL 9 μL of sediment was pipetted on microscopic slide and examined with 24 × 32 mm cover slides (Isolab, Germany), each square measuring 0.13–0.17 mm grid. At least 10 microscopic fields were examined under a Carl Zeiss Axiostar binocular bright field light microscope (Serial No: 518G, Göttingen, Germany). Crystals and casts were evaluated using same slide at 100× magnification (Low power field, LPF) and other particles at 400× magnification (High power field, HPF) by two well trained technicians and a clinical laboratory specialist with at least 5 years of experience in urine microscopy. For minimizing inter-observer variability, microscopic examination was performed independently within 1 h using the same microscope. Same technician performed all the microscopic sediment examination with the same microscope by using the KOVA® system (Hycor Biomedical, Garden Grove, CA, USA.). Particle counting was confirmed when at least two out of three independent observers reported same grades of particles on the same microscopic slide. Samples with different evaluations by three independent observers were excluded from the study. Manual phase contrast microscopy of stained (Sternheimer-Alcian blue), uncentrifuged urine with counting chambers such as Fuchs-Rosenthal (optimal), Kova (acceptable) or Burker is considered as gold standard method for microscopic examination. However, most of the clinical laboratories perform microscopic analysis via brightfield microscopy as stated “generally sufficient” in CLSI guideline [ ]. Thus, manual microscopy with brightfield examination was used for confirmation. 2.4 Statistical analysis All statistical calculations were performed with MedCalc Statistical Software version 20.118 (MedCalc Software bv Ostend, Belgium; https://www.medcalc.org ; 2020) and SPSS statistical software package version 21.0. Preliminary examination of the data were assessed according to CLSI EP09 [ ] to detect outliers by Grubbs double-sided, generalized ESD with an alpha level of 0.05. The normality of specific gravity was tested by Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. According to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the p values of urine SG results were 0.0002 and < 0.0001 for FUS-2000 and Tricell-1000, respectively. According to Generalized ESD and Grubbs test, there was 1 outlier value (SG = 1.045) in Tricell-1000 SG results. Distribution of urine specific gravity results was non-parametric. Therefore, spearman correlation analysis was performed [ ]. Comparison of quantitative parameter (Urine specific gravity) was evaluated by Passing-Bablok regression analysis, spearman correlation coefficient (r) and Bland Altman plot (mean of both methods against plot differences). Within-run (20 replicates for each level of urine controls in the same batch) and between-run (4 replicates for each level of urine controls for 5 days) precision experiments for urine microscopy (RBC and WBC) were performed with Cliniqa Liquid QC DipScopics Control (Lot No:2204178, San Marcos, USA). Mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation (CV) values were calculated by using Microsoft Excel v16.0.15831.20,098. Concordance rate (%), concordance rate (%) with ±1 grading difference rates (%) and weighted kappa values for agreement were calculated for strip chemical parameters. Minimum [(kappa coefficients (ϰ) >0.6] and optimal [(kappa coefficients (ϰ) >0.8, if achievable] performance specifications were defined in European Urinalysis Guideline (7). For urine sediment comparison; red blood cell (RBC), white blood cell (WBC), squamous epithelial cells (SEC), bacteria (BAC) were classified semi-quantitatively (0–5, 6–10, 11–20, and >20 cells/HPF) and other particles like calcium oxalate crystals (CaOx), amorphous phosphate crystals (AP) and yeast like cells (YLC), hyaline casts (HC), granular casts (GC), leukocyte clusters (LC), mucous thread (MT) and renal tubular epithelial cells (RTEC) (detected or not detected) [ ]. Cohen's kappa coefficients (ϰ) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for concordance between methods [ ] and values of 0–0.21, 0.21–0.40, 0.40–0.60, 0.61–0.80 and 0.81–1.00 are characterized with a statistical perspective as poor, fair, moderate, good, and very good agreement, respectively [ ]. Cohen's kappa coefficients (ϰ) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for concordance between methods [ ] and values of 0–0.21, 0.21–0.40, 0.40–0.60, 0.61–0.80 and 0.81–1.00 are characterized with a statistical perspective as poor, fair, moderate, good, and very good agreement, respectively [ ]. In clinical assessment, weighted kappa values (4–5 classes such as WBC, RBC, SEC and BAC in this study) were accepted as >0.7 and > 0.9 for minimum and optimum analytical quality goal in European Urinalysis Guideline [ ]. Concordance rate (%), concordance rate ±1 grading difference (%), sensitivity, specificity, negative and positive predictive values (NPV and PPV, respectively), area under curve (AUC), Positive Likelihood Ratio (PLR) and Negative Likelihood Ratio (NLR) according to manual microscopy (reference method) were calculated by using MedCalc statistical software. Statistical significance was considered at the level of p < 0.05. 3 Results According to Passing-Bablok regression analysis, spearman correlation coefficient and regression equation (458 urine samples included) of urine specific gravity (SG) were as 0.934 and (Tricell-1000 SG) = 0.9728 (95% CI: 0.9239 to 1.0217) x (FUS-2000 SG) + 0.02269 (95% CI: 0.02692 to 0.07229). For urine specific gravity comparison, the slope and intercept 95% CI intervals in the regression equation included a value of 1 and 0, respectively. In a study with a sample size of 200–500, at least 93% results of the samples must be within the Bland Altman confidence interval (CI) [ ]. In this study, 94.1% of the urine SG values were within the CI range. Even though automated urine devices have a SG test pad on the strip, most of the systems perform SG measurement with a refractometer. The Bland Altman plot demonstrated an acceptable systematic constant bias of 0.005 units between the Tricell-1000 and FUS-2000 systems ( ). This bias was acceptable compared to total allowable error for urine specific gravity (0.01 unit) [ ]. Median (25–75%) quartile values for SG were calculated as 1.017 (1.011–1.022) and 1.012 (1.006–1.017) for FUS-2000 and Tricell-1000 SG results (p < 0.0001). Urine SG results of both systems presented a strong correlation with a 0.934 spearman correlation coefficient. Bland Altman plot (left) and Passing-Bablok (right) was presented in . For precision analysis of microscopic RBC and WBC, within- and between run CV values for RBC and WBC ranged between 6.4 and 24.1 vs 9.45–30.3% and 7.25–26.0 vs 8.08–23.7% for TRISED-100 and FUS-200, respectively ( ). According to chemical strip comparison between two devices, concordance rates were 30%, 88%, 87%, 98%, 100%, 70%, 97%,99%,73% for pH, glucose, protein, bilirubin, urobilinogen, blood, ketone, nitrite and leukocyte esterase, respectively. Agreement between two strips were optimal for glucose [(ϰ = 0.84(0.81–0.86)], urobilinogen, [(ϰ = 1.00 (1.00–1.00)], ketone [(ϰ = 0.81 (0.70–0.92)], nitrite [(ϰ = 0.95(0.85–1.00)]; acceptable for blood [(ϰ = 0.62 (0.56–0.67)], leukocyte esterase [(ϰ = 0.77 (0.73–0.81)]; fair for pH [(ϰ = 0.43 (0.38–0.48)], protein [(ϰ = 0.49 (0.43–0.56)] and poor for bilirubin [(ϰ = 0.14 (−0.07-0.35] ( ). Concordance rates, concordance rates ±1 grading units and weighted kappa values for microscopic comparison were presented in . Concordance of Tricell-100 with manual microscopy was higher for sediment RBC (92% vs 83%), WBC (90% vs 82%), SEC (91% vs 86%), CaOx (96% vs 93%), YLC (99% vs 98%), HC (97% vs 96%) and MT (78% vs 65%) compared to FUS-200, respectively. FUS-200 yielded more concordant results with manual microscopy for bacteria (71% vs 68%), LC (96% vs 95%) and RTEC (98% vs 97%) than Tricell-100, respectively. Concordance rates for AP and GC were similar for both systems (92% and 98%, respectively). According to these ratios, concordance above 80% was found in all other parameters except bacteria and mucous thread in microscopic imaging. According to Cohen's kappa coefficients (ϰ), agreement between Tricell-100 and manual microscopy was very good for RBC (ϰ = 0.80), and WBC (ϰ = 0.83); good for CaOx (ϰ = 0.69), SEC (ϰ = 0.80), YLC (ϰ = 0.72), HC (0.69) and LC (ϰ = 0.64); moderate for BAC (ϰ = 0.51), AP (ϰ = 0.43) and MT (ϰ = 0.55); fair for GC (ϰ = 0.39) and RTEC (ϰ = 0.32). Agreement between FUS-200 and manual microscopy was good for WBC (ϰ = 0.68), SEC (ϰ = 0.70), BAC (ϰ = 0.62) and LC (ϰ = 0.69); moderate for RBC (ϰ = 0.56), CaOx (ϰ = 0.44), AP (ϰ = 0.50), YLC (ϰ = 0.56) and HC (ϰ = 0.46); fair for GC (ϰ = 0.24), MT (ϰ = 0.32) and RTEC (ϰ = 0.35). Agreement between FUS-200 and manual microscopy was good for WBC (ϰ = 0.68), SEC (ϰ = 0.70), BAC (ϰ = 0.62) and LC (ϰ = 0.69); moderate for RBC (ϰ = 0.56), CaOx (ϰ = 0.44), AP (ϰ = 0.50), YLC (ϰ = 0.56) and HC (ϰ = 0.46); fair for GC (ϰ = 0.24), MT (ϰ = 0.32) and RTEC (ϰ = 0.35). Specificity values of Tricell-100 sediment RBC, WBC, SEC, BAC, CaOx, AP and YLC were higher than FUS-200 (94.4% vs 87.7%; 96.2% vs 88.0%; 94.7% vs 93.1%; 89.2% vs 85.1%; 100% vs 99.5%; 98.5% vs 97.6% and 100% vs 99.3%, respectively). FUS-200 yielded more sensitive results for WBC (97.7% vs 94.3%). Sensitivity% values were same in both systems for sediment RBC (89.5% vs 89.5%). Sensitivity values of HC, GC and RTEC were markedly lower for Tricell-100 and FUS-200 (68.4% vs 36.8%; 28.5% vs 14.2% and 42.8% vs 28.5%, respectively). Diagnostic performance specifications were presented in . 4 Discussion The combination of automated urine systems sediment and chemical strip analysis allows the laboratory a high throughput and minimal technician intervention. In addition to shortening the turnaround time, a more standardized urine analysis can be performed. For urine sediment assessments, higher CV values were reported in manual microscopy (up to 100%). The authors even described manual microscopy as a “qualitative reference method” [ ]. In contrast to manual microscopy, CV values are lower in automated systems. Due to different composition of cell counts in control materials, CV values ranged between 10 and 40%. The CV values of microscopic RBC and WBC in this study ( ) were consistent with previous studies [ , , ] Manual microscopy generates less precise results compared to automated urine analyzers. The possible cause of this imprecision might be due to non-standardized preanalytical steps and inaccurate particle counting (subjective interpretation) in manual microscopy [ ]. Based on our chemical strip performance evaluation in this study, the concordance rate for strip pH was not satisfactory ( ). In previous studies, discordant results (41% concordance rate for pH) were also reported for Sysmex UX-2000 vs Cobas 6500 [ ] and Cobas 6500 (Cobas u601) vs Sysmex UN3000-111b (UC-3500) systems. Although pH was comparable, urobilinogen and bilirubin demonstrated poor performance for Cobas 6500 and Iris IQ200 test strips [ ]. In a study, a concordance level of approximately 80% was obtained for all parameters with Atlas and Urisys strips [ ]. Nonetheless, agreement between strips were comparable for other parameters. An overall agreement of 80% were accepted as satisfactory for strip parameters [ ]. According to kappa coefficients, there was a fair agreement for protein [(ϰ = 0.49 (0.43–0.56)] between two strips. Differences for strip parameters might be due to altered chemical design of pads, the calibration of readers for optical absorbance or interferences from higher levels of urinary glucose, protein and drugs etc. An optimal agreement for urobilinogen, [(ϰ = 1.00 (1.00–1.00)] and poor agreement for bilirubin [(ϰ = 0.14 (−0.07-0.35] was obtained ( ). These results might be conflicting due to small number of positive samples in this study. 0.2 % vs 2% and 0.4% vs 0.4% of total samples were detected as positive for bilirubin and urobilinogen in Tricell-1000 and FUS-2000 platforms. Although measurement of urine urobilinogen and bilirubin levels have no importance in detecting liver disease anymore [ ], strip agreements for these parameters should be verified by large number of positive samples. According to sediment analysis ( ), TriCell-1000 and FUS-2000 showed very good performance (concordance rates >80%) in comparison to manual microscopy except bacteria and mucous thread (65–78% concordance rates). Falbo et al. [ ] reported similar results for bacteria (69%) and mucous (71%) on sediMAX conTRUST PRO (77 Elektronica, Budapest, Hungary) platform. Low concordance rates for bacteria (51%) were also reported for Iris iQ200 and Sysmex UF100 [ ]. Urinalysis is first step screening test in clinical suspicion of urinary tract infection (UTI). A positive result of nitrite and leukocyte esterase on urine chemical analysis and the detection of a significant amount of bacteria and leukocytes on sediment examination lead to urine culture for microbiological examination (gold standard) [ ]. The cause of discrepancy might be due to misclassification of bacteria in different shapes and sizes in the urine sample. Since urine screening is a semiquantitative method, even detecting the presence of bacteria may provide an important diagnostic data for especially “rule-out” of UTI. Even if the screening result is negative, culture should be performed in children, pregnant women and immunosuppressed patients [ ]. and leukocytes on sediment examination lead to urine culture for microbiological examination (gold standard) [ ]. The cause of discrepancy might be due to misclassification of bacteria in different shapes and sizes in the urine sample. Since urine screening is a semiquantitative method, even detecting the presence of bacteria may provide an important diagnostic data for especially “rule-out” of UTI. Even if the screening result is negative, culture should be performed in children, pregnant women and immunosuppressed patients [ ]. Inadequate identification of bacteria has been a problem with previous image-based systems on the market [ ]. Flow cytometry-based urine sediment analyzers including dedicated bacterial channel have even been introduced to overcome this problem and reduce the need for urine culture [ ]. Although manual urine microscopy has high variability, examination of urine sediment for the discrimination of small particles via bright field microscopy by an experienced technician may be enlightening. In fact, one of the main problems of urine sediment analyzers is the inability to distinguish between erythrocytes and small particles such as yeasts, bacteria, crystals, dysmorphic cells, amorphous and decomposed parts of cell debris in the sediment [ ]. Clumping of erythrocytes, especially in urine with macroscopic haematuria, may also lead to misclassification with budding yeasts and crystals [ ]. Although most particle analyzers inject a bolus of air for sample homogenization, verification by manual microscopy may be useful for samples with high cell counts. Kouri et al. [ ] reported a weighed kappa value of 0.59 for casts [(combined as HC (non-pathological) and GC (pathological)]. In this study, kappa values of HC (0.69 vs 0.46) and GC (0.39 vs 0.24) were higher for TriCell-1000 compared to FUS-2000 ( ). These results were comparable with Ince et al. (kappa value = 0.13 for casts) [ ]. Lower kappa values were reported for identification of casts on UF-5000 (0.18 and 0.20 for hyaline and pathological cast, respectively), Cobas u701 (0.08 and 0.38 for hyaline and pathological cast, respectively), UAS800 (0.16 and 0.31 for hyaline and pathological cast, respectively), Iris iQ®200SPRINT (0.04 and “not detected” for hyaline and pathological cast, respectively) and URiSCAN®PlusScope (0.04 and “not detected” for hyaline and pathological cast, respectively) platforms [ ]. Detection of pathological casts in sediment analysis is an important indicator of kidney damage. However, automated systems are insufficient for cast identification [ ]. This may be related to variable structures of cast (due to low refractive index) s and insufficient identification of these particles due to low counts. Even if found with low particle counts, the detection of pathological casts other than hyaline is of great importance for the diagnosis of kidney damage. Therefore, in cases of clinical suspicion, it may be important to screen casts by manual microscopy [ ]. In our study, PPV values for RBC (65.1% vs 45.7% for Tricell-1000 and FUS-200, respectively) and NPV values for bacteria (78.2% vs 79% for Tricell-1000 and FUS-200, respectively) were lower compared to other particles ( ). NPV is an essential feature for avoiding misclassification of positive urine samples as negative. Laiwejpithaya et al. [ ] reported NPV values of bacteria identification as 85.7% and 79.8% for UX-2000 and Urised 3. Lee et al. [ ] concluded NPV values for bacteria as 72.1% and 61.8% for Cobas u701 and UF-1000i. Also, for classification of RBC, Tantisaranon et al. [ ] reported PPV values as 75.8%, 94.4% and 64.9% for Cobas 6500, UN3000-111b and iRICELL 3000 systems, respectively. Falbo et al. [ ] reported PPV value of RBC as 75.2% for sediMAX conTRUST PRO system. These results were similar with this study's results. Examination of unstained urine by bright field microscopy is inadequate for correct identification of bacteria, hyaline casts and RBC [ ]. Also, sensitivity values were lower for casts (68.4% vs 36.8% for hyaline and 28.5% vs 14.2% for granular), yeasts (57.1% vs 57.1%), crystals (55% vs 32.5% for CaOx and 34.7% vs 45.6% for AP) for Tricell-1000 and FUS-2000, respectively ( ). This is a major dilemma for automated sediment analyzers. In the case of low number of RBC or presence of yeasts, crystals, cell clumping in urine sediment, devices suffer from identification of these particles with similar structures. Therefore, there is still a reliance on manual microscopy. To overwhelm this issue, either supravital staining of the particles or the use of phase contrast microscopy should be encouraged. Automated urine analyzers provide an improvement in reproducibility and shorten the analysis period and minimize the overall costs. Therefore, characterization of these formed elements should be performed by manual microscopy [ ]. However, these interventions may lead to prolonged turnaround times for urinalysis. In several studies [ , ], authors concluded that automated platforms performed sufficient diagnostic performance for detection of RBC, WBC, SEC, thus can replace manual microscopy. While Tricell-1000 produced higher sensitivity for SEC compared to FUS-2000, FUS-2000 had better diagnostic performance for WBC parameter ( ). These automatized analyzers may be used for a screening strategy to clarify “disease free” population and provide fast results. 5 Conclusion These two automated systems have satisfactory agreement with manual microscopy. Automated analyzers are effective devices for rapid screening of different pathological conditions in routine laboratories. The main aspect of this study was to compare Labsan Trion TriCell-1000 automated urinalysis system with one of the most common systems in our country. Limitations Major limitation of this study was the lack of phase contrast microscopy and staining (for an improvement of particle differentiation) of uncentrifuged urine. The limited number of renal casts (HC and GC) and specific particles (such as RTEC) and lack of reference methods for comparison such as urine culture for bacteria, nitrite, leukocyte esterase; refractometry for SG; dye binding methods for urinary protein; hexokinase method for glucose were other limitations.
